newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-SICILY REMATCH FOR GREEKS AND ROMANS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SICILY REMATCH FOR GREEKS AND ROMANS.

text.p: Sicily, colonised by the Greeks and then conquered by the legions of Imperial Rome, is once again witnessing a battle for supremacy between the twin superpowers of the ancient world.
This time though, the prize at stake in the clash between Athens and Rome is not the island itself, but the right to host the 2004 Olympic Games.
The two Mediterranean capitals are favourites to win the Games. The other short-listed cities are Buenos Aires, Cape Town and Stockholm.
The bidding process reaches a climax on September 5, when the International Olympic Committee (IOC) meets in Lausanne to name the winning candidate.
Between now and then, all eyes will be on the World Student Games, which began this week in Sicily.

A successful Games would boost Rome's chances of hosting the Olympics by proving to the world that Italy's trouble-free organisation of the 1990 World Cup was no fluke, and that the country can hold major sports events anytime, anyplace and anywhere.

But if the Games are as chaotic as many have predicted, the Olympic pendulum could swing towards Athens. The Greek capital earlier this month staged the world athletics championships which were generally perceived as friendly and well organised, if rather poorly attended.

Key to the battle is Italian lawyer Primo Nebiolo, head of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), IOC member, vocal proponent of Rome's bid and the driving force behind the initial move to bring the Student Games to Sicily's shores.
Nebiolo triggered a war of words between the rival candidates at the end of the Athens championships by suggesting that their success was due to IAAF know-how rather than Greek organisational skill.
The Greeks talked of Italy's problem with the Mafia, a particularly sensitive topic of conversation for Sicilians, who responded with jibes about the transport system in Athens.
On Thursday, the Greek delegation said it would not come to Sicily, citing "technical reasons" in a terse statement faxed to the Games organising committee in Palermo.
The Sicilians expressed their bewilderment and disappointment and on Monday, the day before the opening ceremony, the Greeks changed their mind.

Nebiolo, meanwhile, has been touring the island, inspecting facilities and chivvying along organisers who at times appear to have been taken by surprise by the arrival of around 6,000 athletes and hundreds of journalists.

Work was continuing on venues right up until the weekend and the main media centre in Palermo was only inaugurated last week. The fact events are spread across the island -- the first time the Games have not been held in a single city -- has not helped.

Plans for the Games village were scrapped long ago and competitors are housed in plush hotels throughout the island -- fine for them, but hardly in keeping with the Student Games' ideal of camaraderie and cultural interchange.
But Nebiolo is undeterred.

"Though there have been problems, and this is normal for all international events like the Games, we are in the final phase and, as in the past we have been able to overcome all obstacles like they did in Atlanta," he said.
"The Sicilian University Games will have a far better record than Fukuoka (the Japanese host of the 1995 Games), both for the number of nations participating, 175, and the number of athletes."

A full list of entrants has not been made available but the IAAF chief promised appearances by, among others, world long jump champion Ivan Pedroso of Cuba, his compatriot Noberto Tellez, who won the 800 metres silver medal in Athens, and South African Olympic swimming champion Penny Heyns.
Nebiolo also announced a "World Festival of Sprint" to be held in Catania on the final weekend of the Games (August 30-31).
"It will include world-class runners like Michael Johnson, Frank Fredericks, Dennis Mitchell, Leroy Burrell, Merlene Ottey and many others," he said.
That may help the Games end on a high note, just what Rome wants in the run-up to the IOC's September meeting and just what Athens could do without.

The last time Greeks and Romans clashed in Sicily, in the third century B.C., the Roman's scored a decisive victory, driving the Greeks out of the port of Syracuse and claiming the islands for themselves.
The rematch, with the Olympic Games as top prize, starts here.
